def: The single task a language model is trained on and performs: given a sequence of tokens, output a probability for every possible next token. Generation repeats it in a loop.
The vector a token is turned into by looking up its row in a learned table \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}\). Tokens used in similar ways end up with nearby vectors.
The fixed set of tokens a model can read and write, typically 50,000 to 250,000 entries, set by the tokenizer before pretraining.
The repeated unit of a transformer: an attention sublayer then an MLP sublayer, each adding its output to the residual stream. Large models stack 32 to over 100 of them.
The mechanism that lets each position gather information from other positions: it scores its query against every key, softmaxes the scores, and takes the weighted sum of values.
Three learned projections of each position's vector. The query says what a position is looking for, the key what it offers as a match, the value what it hands over when attended to.
\(\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k} + M)V\). Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps scores from growing with vector width.
The matrix that sets attention scores to future positions to \(-\infty\), so each token can only attend to itself and earlier tokens. It lets one training pass make a prediction at every position.
One of several attention computations run in parallel with their own projections. Heads specialise, for example copying the previous token or linking a pronoun to its noun.
An attention head pattern that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and predicts the token that followed it, completing repeated sequences (Olsson et al. 2022).
The tendency of many heads to put most of their weight on the first token when nothing else is relevant, effectively a no-op option (Xiao et al. 2023).
The per-position sublayer \(W_2\,\phi(W_1 x)\) in each transformer block. It holds about two thirds of a dense model's parameters and behaves partly like a key-value memory of associations.
The running vector at each position that every sublayer reads from and adds to. Nothing overwrites it, so later layers can read what earlier layers wrote.
Rescaling a vector to a standard size before each sublayer (often RMSNorm in current models), which keeps training stable in deep stacks.
A way to give attention a sense of order by rotating query and key vectors by an angle proportional to position, so their dot product depends on relative distance.
The final matrix \(W_U\) that maps the last residual vector to one logit per vocabulary token.
Producing text one token at a time, each conditioned on all tokens so far: predict, pick, append, repeat. One forward pass per generated token.
One run of the network from input tokens to output logits. A dense model with \(N\) parameters costs about \(2N\) floating-point operations per token.
The finding that models trained on "A is B" often fail to answer "what is B?" with A (Berglund et al. 2023): stored knowledge is directional.
Evaluating by comparing the log-probabilities a model assigns to fixed answer options, instead of grading text the model generates.
A model after pretraining only. It continues any document in whatever style the document suggests and has no built-in notion of answering a user.
A base model further trained (SFT, then preference training such as RLHF or DPO) to continue conversation-formatted documents in the role of a helpful assistant.
Text placed at the start of a chat, in its own role, that sets instructions, persona or context. To the model it is ordinary tokens that training taught it to weight heavily.
Putting a handful of worked examples in the prompt so that the most likely continuation follows the same pattern. Works on base models without any fine-tuning.
Fluent, plausible output that is false or unsupported, such as an invented citation or a wrong date stated confidently.
Declining to answer, or saying "I don't know", when confidence is too low. Useful only if the grading or reward gives it more credit than a likely-wrong guess.
A confidence the model states in words ("I'm about 70% sure"), as opposed to one read from its token probabilities. Both can be checked for calibration.
A grading rule that tells the model the threshold at which answering pays off, for example "answer only if more than t confident; wrong answers cost t/(1−t) points" (Kalai et al. 2025).
Asking a model to review and fix its own answer. Without new external information it often fails to improve reasoning answers and can make them worse (Huang et al. 2023).
The character a chat model is trained to play (the assistant). It is a learned pattern of text, not a separate agent with goals.
A piece of text (a word, part of a word, or punctuation) with an ID in the model's vocabulary; the unit the model reads and predicts.
The raw score the model outputs for every vocabulary token before softmax; higher means more likely next.
Turns logits into probabilities that sum to 1 by exponentiating and normalising; it depends only on differences between logits.
The text format, with special role tokens, that turns a list of chat messages into the single document the model continues.
Telling users what they seem to want to hear: agreeing with wrong claims, caving when challenged, praising weak work.
Whether stated confidence matches accuracy: answers given at 80% confidence should be right about 80% of the time.
